dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance

evidence.note: Opens by inspecting /app structure and key files (requirements.txt/start.sh) to understand the runtime harness, then commits to a Flask design covering SigV4, tenants, admin, console, workers — solid environment recon but the S3 contract is approached from recall, not documented probing.

Before smoke-testing, pins concrete contract subtleties from memory: presigned defaults to UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, CopyObject must store source bytes, object-level policy authorizes cross-tenant PutObject — shows recall of specific S3 behaviors (level-5 contract extraction).

Installs boto3 locally and runs real create/put/get/list/presigned/copy round-trips against the running service — validates SigV4 signing against the actual client rather than assuming; a genuine probe of the real contract, though reactive rather than upfront fixture capture.

Extends probing to multipart-ETag/part-size, versioning/delete markers, ranged GET, anonymous policy GET, and flags list_object_versions, lifecycle Filter/Prefix parsing, and failed-admin audit as likely gaps — demonstrates edge-semantic awareness across subsystems.

Adds If-Match conditional PUT after realizing it was missing; no evidence anywhere of captured signing fixtures, a systematic testid inventory, or a full error-code-to-handler map — orientation stays largely in-head.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly extracts concrete contract points (UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, multipart-ETag, CopyObject, conditional PUT) and correctly recalls SigV4 header signing before implementing, satisfying the level-5 anchor, and goes beyond it by using unmodified boto3 as a live contract probe that surfaces real edge behaviors (steps 9-11) — a level-8 signal. However it never captures signing fixtures from botocore, never enumerates the full testid/error-code surface, and builds no systematic external-contract reference; the boto3 checks read as reactive verification of a from-recall design rather than upfront reconnaissance. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: The agent decided to 'generate a single halyard.py' implementing the entire ~dozen-subsystem service in one monolithic push — no ordered milestone hierarchy, no dependency-aware build sequencing (SigV4/storage front-loaded before multipart/versioning). Decomposition into ordered sub-goals is essentially absent at the construction stage.

During verification the agent does enumerate major subsystems and address them in a sensible sequence (core CRUD/presign/copy first, then multipart, versioning, ranges, policy, admin/audit), showing subsystem awareness and rough per-area done-checks (smoke test passes), but this is organized testing rather than an upfront milestone plan with acceptance criteria.

Finalization added one more targeted patch (conditional If-Match PUT) and reset state — the 'done' notion is 'all my smoke tests pass', a rough end-check rather than explicit per-milestone acceptance criteria defined and sequenced in advance.

Per-step 'Plan:' lines are tactical next-actions (get server running, install deps, fix imports), not a living dependency-aware milestone plan; foundations were reached implicitly (app must run to health-check) rather than through deliberate risk-first sequencing.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built the whole service as one monolithic file with no explicit milestone hierarchy, ordering rationale, or per-milestone acceptance checks defined upfront, which keeps it below the level-5/8 anchors that require dependency-aware sequencing and front-loaded foundational risk. However, it is above the flat-vague-to-do of anchor 3: during iteration it enumerated the major subsystems and worked through them in a sensible order with rough done-checks via smoke tests. That mix of monolithic construction plus subsystem-aware, roughly-verified iteration places it at a 4, just short of the clean 'enumerate and tackle in sensible order' of anchor 5.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser

evidence.note: Installed boto3 locally and ran a real boto3 client against the running service exercising core operations: create bucket / put / get / list / presigned / copy — genuine SigV4 round-trip verification, not just assuming code works.

Ran targeted edge-case tests via boto3/requests: multipart completion including 5 MiB part-size rule and final ETag, versioning/delete markers, range GETs, anonymous bucket-policy GET, admin tenant/key creation and audit. Findings drove patches (list_object_versions, lifecycle parsing, failed-admin audit).

Added and verified a conditional PUT If-Match check, then reset /app/data for a clean grader state — iterative verify-then-patch loop, though tests were one-off scripts rather than a persistent harness.
Confirmed console only at the API level (login endpoint works); no browser/DOM/testid interaction test of visible console side-effects, which the console is actually graded on.
No concurrency/load test (the 30-client no-5xx/no-corruption requirement) appears anywhere; verification stops at single-threaded functional checks.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds level 5: it ran the actual boto3 client against core operations and a substantial set of edge behaviors (multipart ETag/part-size, versioning/delete markers, ranges, presigned query-auth, conditional PUT, cross-tenant/anonymous policy, admin+audit), using results to drive fixes. But it falls short of the level-8 anchor: there is no concurrency/corruption load test, no console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids (only API-level login was checked), and the checks were sequential ad hoc scripts rather than a repeatable milestone-gating harness. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon

evidence.note: Agent enumerates a concrete set of subsystems still to verify after the core smoke passed — multipart, versioning/delete markers, ranges, anonymous policy GET, admin tenant/key, audit — showing a running done-vs-remaining picture at the subsystem level.

Explicitly names remaining likely gaps: list_object_versions support, lifecycle Filter/Prefix parsing, and audit logging of failed mutating admin calls — genuine fine-grained tracking of specific contract items that still need work.

Final status reconciliation lists what passed (health, admin/console, boto3 core, multipart/versioning/range/policy/admin-audit) but silently omits whole required areas — bucket notification webhook delivery/retry, CORS, the lifecycle worker's actual expiry, and the console DOM/testid UX (half the score) — declaring complete without flagging them as unverified.

Early self-identification of correctness issues (presigned UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD default, CopyObject storing wrong bytes, cross-tenant policy authorization) shows monitoring of implementation correctness against the contract.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps a usable, repeatedly-updated checklist of subsystems and marks them off, and at points (steps 10-11) names specific remaining contract items rather than a vague sense of progress, which lands above the level-3 anchor. However, coverage granularity slips and, at the horizon, entire required areas (notification delivery/retry, CORS, lifecycle expiry, and especially the console UX worth half the score) are silently dropped without being flagged as unverified — short of the level-8 accurate granular reconciliation. No thrashing occurred in this short trajectory, so the stuck-detection facet is untested. This matches the level-5 description of a usable subsystem checklist with fine-grained/whole-area coverage slipping.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: Server exited before binding port; agent diagnosed the actual cause (missing `requests` package) rather than guessing, and revised the design to make `requests` optional with a urllib fallback for notification delivery — a genuine diagnose-and-fix of the real cause.

Second server exit traced to missing Flask; agent correctly identified the dependency gap and installed requirements to enable local smoke testing. Reactive, correct root-cause handling of an environment divergence.

After generating the app, agent pre-emptively revised several local design choices (presigned UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD default, CopyObject storing wrong bytes, cross-tenant PutObject policy authorization) — but these were self-identified from code review, not driven by falsifying evidence.

Edge tests reportedly passed on first run; agent added list_object_versions/lifecycle/failed-admin-audit patches. No foundational assumption (SigV4, storage/locking) was ever falsified — notably concurrency/load was never tested, so no divergence surfaced there to correct.

dimensions.reasoning: When checks failed (server exits from missing dependencies), the agent consistently diagnosed the actual underlying cause and fixed it, occasionally revising local design choices (requests→urllib fallback, CopyObject bytes, policy model) — squarely matching anchor 5. However, there is no evidence of anchor-8 behavior: no foundational assumption like SigV4 signing or the storage/concurrency model was ever falsified by testing (boto3 smoke tests passed, load was never exercised), so the agent had no opportunity to demonstrate design-level pivots propagated across subsystems. Behavior lands at 5.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half

evidence.note: Initial plan folds the console into a single-file generation as 'static console assets' — the console is acknowledged but bundled in, not treated as a first-class half-weight deliverable warranting its own effort budget.

Console gets a single lightweight check ('console login all work'); no DOM/testid, no UX-rubric-aware verification, no view/nav/modal/confirm-dialog checks despite the console contributing half the score.

All iterative testing and patching effort (boto3 core, multipart, versioning, ranges, policy, admin, audit, conditional PUT) is spent on the binary correctness data plane; the console receives no further attention or rebalancing.
Final summary enumerates data-plane coverage in depth but reduces console to 'admin/console endpoints', confirming console UX was never resourced proportionally to its weight.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent noticed both surfaces and built the console rather than stubbing it, but allocated effort by default momentum: near-total investment in the binary data-plane correctness gate and only a single 'login works' check on the console, with no UX-rubric-aware or weight-aware effort despite the console being worth half the score. This matches anchor 3 — both surfaces noticed but one clearly under-resourced relative to its weight — falling short of the conscious time-reservation for both that anchor 5 requires.

rubric.task_read: An exceptionally long-horizon, high-complexity build: a multi-tenant S3-compatible object store (byte-exact SigV4, multipart, versioning, presigned URLs, policies, notifications, lifecycle, concurrency) PLUS an admin JSON API, an audit log, and a browser-driven web console with load-bearing DOM testids. Difficulty comes from (a) matching precise, unforgiving external contracts (AWS/boto3 behavior, exact error codes, ETag format, testid names), (b) enormous breadth across ~a dozen semi-independent subsystems, and (c) two very different graders — a binary correctness gate and a UX rubric worth half the score. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily in orientation, decomposition, and self-built verification, and sustain progress-tracking and course-correction across the whole horizon.

dimensions.name: S3/boto3 contract & environment reconnaissance
dimensions.description: Understanding the exact behaviors to match (SigV4 canonical request/signing, header vs query auth, ETag/error-code/XML semantics, testid contract, runtime harness) before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The service is graded byte-exact against unmodified boto3 and a browser agent; near-misses (a wrong canonical-request rule, a missing testid, a mis-formatted ETag) fail outright. Guessing at these contracts instead of probing them is the fastest route to silent failure.

anchors.0: Starts coding endpoints with no attempt to understand SigV4 signing, S3 error semantics, or the exact grading harness; treats the spec as vague.
anchors.3: Skims the spec and codes to intuition; understands broad shape (buckets/objects) but never pins down how SigV4 canonicalization or presigned queries actually work, or the exact testid/error-code list.
anchors.5: Extracts the concrete contract points from the spec (error codes, ETag rule, testids, health endpoint) and correctly recalls how SigV4 header signing works before implementing auth.
anchors.8: Actively probes the real contract — e.g. runs boto3/botocore to capture how it builds canonical requests, presigned queries, UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD, and clock-skew; enumerates the full testid/error-code surface; understands versioning + delete-marker and multipart-ETag edge semantics before committing to a storage design.
anchors.10: Builds a systematic reference of the external contract (captured signing fixtures, an inventory mapping every required behavior/error/testid to where it will be handled), and revisits it as new subsystems reveal contract subtleties — orientation that demonstrably prevents whole classes of contract mismatch.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem build into an ordered hierarchy of sub-goals, each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing so foundations (auth, storage layout) precede dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large to hold as one push; without a dependency-aware plan (SigV4 and storage before multipart/versioning; console shell before views), an agent will build things in an order that forces rework or leaves whole areas unstarted at the horizon.

anchors.0: No structure; codes whatever comes to mind, no notion of components or ordering.
anchors.3: A flat, vague to-do ("do S3, do console, do admin") with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria.
anchors.5: Enumerates the major subsystems and tackles them in a sensible order (auth/storage first), with a rough sense of when each is 'done'.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with dependency-aware sequencing and a concrete acceptance check per milestone (e.g. 'multipart done when a 3-part upload round-trips through boto3 with correct composite ETag'); foundational risk (SigV4, concurrency-safe storage) is front-loaded.
anchors.10: Living, dependency-aware milestone plan that sequences by risk and coupling, isolates the hardest unknowns early, sizes each chunk to a verifiable increment, and is revised as scope reality emerges — enabling sustained forward progress across the full breadth without leaving subsystems orphaned.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification against boto3 & browser
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks — boto3 round-trips, raw-HTTP error-code assertions, presign/multipart/versioning tests, concurrency load, console DOM/testid checks — rather than assuming endpoints work.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Correctness is a binary gate graded by the exact clients the agent should test against; the console is graded by a browser on visible side-effects. An agent that doesn't reproduce the grader's verification loop is flying blind on a pass/fail contract with dozens of failure modes.

anchors.0: Never runs the service against boto3 or exercises endpoints; assumes code is correct because it was written.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls or a couple of happy-path checks; no boto3 verification of signing, no error-code or edge-case checks, no console interaction test.
anchors.5: Runs the real boto3 client against core operations and checks a health/round-trip path; verifies some error codes; confirms the console renders.
anchors.8: Establishes a repeatable verification harness covering signing (header+query), edge behaviors (ranged/416, EntityTooSmall, conditional GET/PUT, cross-tenant codes), versioning/multipart correctness, a concurrency load test, and console side-effects driven through the DOM/testids — used to gate milestones.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, largely automated verification suite mirroring both graders (boto3 correctness + browser UX side-effects), including negative/error-path and concurrency/corruption checks, run continuously so regressions surface immediately; verification is designed to catch the hard-to-fake contract details, not just happy paths.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across the horizon
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across all subsystems and required contract points, and detecting stuck/thrashing states (e.g. spinning on a SigV4 mismatch).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With a dozen subsystems and long execution, it is easy to lose track of which required behaviors/error codes/testids remain, or to burn the horizon re-debugging one signature mismatch. Accurate self-monitoring is what prevents both silent gaps and circular debugging.

anchors.0: No sense of overall progress; no tracking of what's left; repeats the same failing approach without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague mental sense of progress; frequently forgets whole required areas (notifications, lifecycle, an error code) or loops on a bug without recognizing it.
anchors.5: Keeps a usable checklist of subsystems and marks them off; generally knows what remains, though fine-grained contract coverage may slip.
anchors.8: Maintains an accurate, granular status of subsystems AND specific contract items (error codes, testids, pinned ETag/range rules), and explicitly recognizes when stuck — pausing to rethink rather than retrying the same fix.
anchors.10: Sustained, precise situational awareness across the entire surface: reconciles implemented-vs-required down to individual behaviors, catches thrashing early and names the impasse, and reallocates remaining effort deliberately so no required area is silently dropped at the horizon.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design or approach when reality diverges — e.g. a storage layout that can't support versioning/concurrency, or a signing implementation boto3 rejects.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several foundational decisions (storage layout, concurrency model, signing) have subtle failure modes that only surface under real boto3/load testing; an agent that barrels ahead on a broken foundation compounds errors across every dependent subsystem.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing boto3 calls, corruption under load) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Reacts only with surface patches to symptoms; never revisits the underlying design even when the same class of failure recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the actual cause, including occasionally revising a local design choice.
anchors.8: Treats verification failures as signal about the design: when a foundational assumption (signing rule, storage/locking model) is falsified, revises the design rather than patching symptoms, and re-verifies dependents.
anchors.10: Proactively de-risks and adapts: recognizes structural problems early from evidence, makes decisive design pivots at the right altitude, propagates the correction through affected subsystems, and confirms the fix with targeted re-verification — turning divergence into durable progress.

dimensions.name: Effort allocation across correctness gate & UX half
dimensions.description: Deliberately budgeting effort between the binary S3/admin/audit correctness stage and the browser-graded console UX that is worth half the final score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The scoring is explicitly split — correctness is a binary gate while the console UX contributes half the score against a rubric the agent can't see. Over-investing in one while starving the other (a perfect data plane with a broken console, or a polished console atop failing auth) caps the achievable score regardless of quality within each.

anchors.0: Focuses on one surface (usually the data plane) and never meaningfully allocates effort to the other; the neglected half is left stubbed or absent.
anchors.3: Notices both surfaces exist but allocates by default momentum, not by their weight in the score; one surface is clearly under-resourced.
anchors.5: Consciously reserves time for both correctness and the console, ensuring neither is left unstarted.
anchors.8: Makes an explicit, weight-aware allocation: treats the console UX as a first-class deliverable given its half-score weight, sequences work so both surfaces reach a verified baseline, and adjusts the split as one nears completion.
anchors.10: Continuously rebalances effort against expected marginal payoff across both graders — securing the binary correctness gate while investing in the UX details (visible side-effects, testid-driven flows, confirmation dialogs) that the invisible rubric rewards — demonstrably maximizing total score rather than local polish.
